answers: Archaeologists in Bulgaria think they've found ashes belonging to one of the 12 apostles. The team found a small lead container with ashes while excavating a basilica that dates back to the sixth century AD, reports Archaeology in Bulgaria. The markings on the inch-long vessel match those at the grave of St. John the Apostle in what is now Turkey, leading researchers to surmise that a long-ago Christian from Bulgaria traveled to the grave site and returned home with the sample of ashes. Such journeys were common around that time, reports Novinite. “Probably a pilgrim from the Foros Peninsula went on a pilgrimage to Ephesus, and came back here with this relic, which was then donated to the basilica on Foros,” says the director of the Burgas Regional Museum of History in Bulgaria. (The ancient basilica is located in what is now the Black Sea city of Burgas.) Archeologists also found a Bulgarian royal seal from the 10th century at the dig site, which includes a fortress, notes the Week. (Another archaeological discovery: an ancient underground city in Turkey.)

full.prediction:
**Summary of News Passages**

In a significant archaeological discovery, Bulgarian archaeologists have uncovered a 6th-century lead vessel containing ashes from the alleged grave of John the Apostle, one of Jesus Christ's twelve apostles, at the ancient and medieval fortress site of Burgos (Poros) on Cape Foros in Burgas, Bulgaria. The reliquary, which is less than an inch long and decorated with crosses, was found within the ruins of an early Christian basilica. This discovery has been hailed as one of the most important in the history of the Burgas Regional Museum of History by Milen Nikolov, the museum's director.

The reliquary is believed to have been brought back from the grave of John the Apostle in Ephesus, Turkey, by a pilgrim from the region. This aligns with the historical practice of early Christians who often carried relics from pilgrimage sites, believing them to have healing properties. The site of John the Apostle's grave in Ephesus was a major pilgrimage destination, and it was said that on the anniversary of his death, a miraculous powder known as manna would appear on the site, believed to have curative powers.

In addition to the reliquary, the excavations at Burgos (Poros) revealed a 10th-century Bulgarian royal seal and other historical artifacts, including a Late Antiquity latrine and remnants of a Roman villa from the 3rd century AD. The site, which has been under excavation since 2008, has also yielded a 6th-century basilica and evidence of its use by various empires, including the Roman, Byzantine, Bulgarian, and Ottoman Empires.

This discovery is not the only significant relic find in the region. In 2010, a reliquary containing relics of St. John the Baptist was discovered on St. Ivan (St. John) Island, near Sozopol, Bulgaria. These relics, which include bone fragments, were later confirmed by Oxford University scholars to be from a man who lived during the time of Jesus Christ.

The lead tube reliquary found in Burgas is unique in that its imagery matches that of clay tube reliquaries produced in ancient Ephesus, suggesting a direct connection to the pilgrimage site. This reinforces the belief that the reliquary was brought back from Ephesus by a pilgrim and later donated to the basilica in Burgas.

These findings highlight the rich historical and religious significance of the region, underscoring its role as a center
